origin_region: Lankaran-Astara region (Lankaran, Astara, Masalli and Lerik districts)
cultivar: Seed-grown bushes of Georgian and Chinese origin from the Soviet plantings, with newer imported clones in the replanted gardens
processing: Orthodox and rotorvane black tea: withered, rolled, fully oxidised and fired, sorted into broken and whole-leaf grades; the big domestic brands blend local leaf with imported tea and often add bergamot or thyme for the local taste.
harvest_season: May to September in the humid subtropical strip along the Caspian, with the May and June picks the best; the bushes rest over the cold winter.
appearance_dry: Dark, fairly fine broken leaf with some longer twisted pieces and reddish stems; a plain, sweet aroma.
appearance_liquor: Deep red-amber, clear, poured from a concentrate.
appearance_wet: Even copper-brown leaf, small to medium.
taste_profile: Strong, dark and fairly brisk with a mild maltiness and a plain sweetness, less harsh than Assam and heavier than Iranian tea; it is made to be drunk hot and strong with sugar or jam.

brewing.notes: Azerbaijani style: a strong concentrate brewed in a small pot on a samovar or kettle, diluted in a pear-shaped armudu glass and served with lemon, sugar cubes, jam and sweets; sometimes a sprig of thyme or a pinch of cloves goes in the pot. No milk.

vintage_note: Sold all year by brand and grade, blended and undated; Azerçay and other national brands dominate and mix Lankaran leaf with imported tea, while a few local producers sell 100% Lankaran tea, sometimes by the May harvest. Use within the year; nothing here is aged.
description:
Azerbaijan's tea grows on a narrow, humid strip of the Caspian coast in the far south, around Lankaran and Astara, where the Talysh mountains catch the rain and the winters are mild. Tea was tried here in the 1880s and planted seriously under the Soviet Union, when Lankaran tea was a minor but proud cousin of the Georgian industry; after 1991 the plantations shrank badly, and the state has spent the last decade trying to replant them.

The leaf is orthodox black tea, fairly strong and plain, and it goes into a national tea culture that matters more than the farming: tea is the first thing offered to any guest, and a samovar, a tray of armudu glasses, lemon, sugar cubes and several jams are the furniture of every Azerbaijani visit. The concentrate is kept warm on the samovar and diluted glass by glass; the pear-shaped glass keeps the bottom hot and the rim cool. Nobody adds milk.

In the glass it is strong, dark and brisk with a mild maltiness and a plain sweetness, closer to a Turkish or a plain Ceylon tea than to anything delicate; good Lankaran leaf from the May harvest is noticeably softer and sweeter. It is often flavoured at the pot with thyme or cloves, and the national brands sell bergamot and thyme blends alongside the plain tea.

Buy it with the understanding that the big brands, Azerçay above all, blend local and imported leaf and do not date their tea; a pack that says 100% Lankaran, ideally from a named local factory and the spring harvest, is the one to seek out. Abroad it is found in Azerbaijani and Turkish groceries and through the national brands' exports.

Drink it the way the country does, with a spoon of quince or walnut jam on the side rather than in the glass, and a slice of lemon; and compare it with Lahijan tea from just over the Iranian border to taste what a few hundred kilometres of coast and a different brewing habit do.
sources_note: First plantings in the 1880s follow the Wikipedia article on tea growing in Azerbaijan; Soviet-era expansion and post-1991 decline are from general history. Azerçay blending local with imported leaf is widely reported but the proportions are not public. Taste tag 'bitter' refers to the strong style as usually brewed.
